result.markdown: --- title: "High dimensions" subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl on grids of two to five dimensions" engine: julia --- Interpolation on tensor-product grids as the number of dimensions grows: the convolution kernels against the linear and cubic B-spline interpolants of Interpolations.jl, the one other package that interpolates on grids in any dimension. A separable kernel of width $w$ per axis touches $w^N$ grid values per evaluation, so the cost of a wide kernel grows fast with the dimension while its accuracy does not: this page measures both. First the cost and the accuracy of every method at the same per-axis resolution from two to five dimensions, then convergence and time to accuracy in three dimensions, and finally lazy construction, which is what makes large grids in many dimensions affordable to build at all. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Packages, the methods and the test function"} using ConvolutionInterpolations import Interpolations using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie # the test function: the N-dimensional Runge function with a mild parameter, non-separable and # smooth on [-1, 1]^N, so that the coarse grids a high-dimensional study can afford resolve it f(x...) = 1 / (1 + sum(abs2, x)) # the grid: n knots per axis on [-1, 1], in N dimensions, and the values on it axes_nd(N, n) = ntuple(_ -> range(-1.0, 1.0, length = n), N) values_nd(N, n) = [f(x...) for x in Iterators.product(axes_nd(N, n)...)] # each method maps the axes and the values to a callable interpolant of N arguments; the # stencil width per axis is what the cost per evaluation grows with, as width^N methods_nd = [ "Interpolations.jl linear" => (ax, v) -> Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(v, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Linear())), ax...), "Interpolations.jl cubic" => (ax, v) -> Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(v, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), ax...), "ConvInterp :a3" => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :a3), "ConvInterp :a4" => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :a4), "ConvInterp :b5" => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b5), "ConvInterp :b7" => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b7), ] width = Dict("Interpolations.jl linear" => 2, "Interpolations.jl cubic" => 4, "ConvInterp :a3" => 4, "ConvInterp :a4" => 6, "ConvInterp :b5" => 10, "ConvInterp :b7" => 12) # m random test points inside the grid, as an N × m matrix, and the exact values there; the # points stay two percent clear of the boundary, so that the methods' different boundary rules # do not decide the error function testpoints(N, m) P = 0.98 .* (2 .* rand(MersenneTwister(1), N, m) .- 1) (P = P, exact = [f(p...) for p in eachcol(P)]) end # evaluate an interpolant at every column of P evalpts(itp, P) = [itp(p...) for p in eachcol(P)] fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) : t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) : t < 1 ? @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f s", t); ``` ::: ## Cost and accuracy against dimension Sixteen knots per axis, from two dimensions (256 grid values) to five (a million), every method built on the same grids and evaluated at ten thousand random points. The time to construct, the time per evaluation, and the largest error against the function. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The dimension study"} Ns = 2:5 n_axis = 16 m_test = 10_000 res = Dict() # (name, N) => (setup, query per point, error) for N in Ns ax = axes_nd(N, n_axis); v = values_nd(N, n_axis) tp = testpoints(N, m_test) for (name, m) in methods_nd itp = m(ax, v) res[(name, N)] = (setup = (@b $m($ax, $v)).time, query = (@b evalpts($itp, $(tp.P))).time / m_test, err = maximum(abs.(evalpts(itp, tp.P) .- tp.exact))) end end fig = Figure(size = (800, 440)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; yscale = log10, xlabel = "dimension", ylabel = "time per evaluation [s]", xticks = Ns) for (name, _) in methods_nd scatterlines!(ax1, Ns, [res[(name, N)].query for N in Ns]; markersize = 8, label = name) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax1) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | time per evaluation | stencil | 2D | 3D | 4D | 5D | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 2ᴺ | 117 ns | 156 ns | 211 ns | 283 ns | | Interpolations.jl cubic | 4ᴺ | 130 ns | 180 ns | 286 ns | 825 ns | | ConvInterp :a3 | 4ᴺ | 114 ns | 159 ns | 338 ns | 1.2 μs | | ConvInterp :a4 | 6ᴺ | 121 ns | 183 ns | 809 ns | 7.3 μs | | ConvInterp :b5 | 10ᴺ | 136 ns | 308 ns | 4.7 μs | 129.2 μs | | ConvInterp :b7 | 12ᴺ | 142 ns | 431 ns | 9.1 μs | 319.2 μs | | construction | 2D | 3D | 4D | 5D | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 167 ns | 1.8 μs | 11.3 μs | 143.45 ms | | Interpolations.jl cubic | 6.5 μs | 69.2 μs | 1.27 ms | 51.86 ms | | ConvInterp :a3 | 6.2 μs | 84.4 μs | 2.14 ms | 53.33 ms | | ConvInterp :a4 | 6.6 μs | 121.1 μs | 3.50 ms | 102.92 ms | | ConvInterp :b5 | 8.9 μs | 273.3 μs | 10.01 ms | 357.94 ms | | ConvInterp :b7 | 12.0 μs | 433.5 μs | 18.01 ms | 736.21 ms | | largest error | 2D | 3D | 4D | 5D | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 8.7e-03 | 1.2e-02 | 1.5e-02 | 1.5e-02 | | Interpolations.jl cubic | 4.4e-04 | 4.4e-04 | 4.3e-04 | 4.0e-04 | | ConvInterp :a3 | 3.6e-04 | 5.0e-04 | 5.8e-04 | 5.1e-04 | | ConvInterp :a4 | 8.5e-05 | 9.4e-05 | 1.0e-04 | 8.5e-05 | | ConvInterp :b5 | 1.1e-05 | 1.1e-05 | 1.1e-05 | 1.0e-05 | | ConvInterp :b7 | 4.7e-06 | 6.6e-06 | 5.9e-06 | 4.1e-06 | In two and three dimensions every method evaluates in a few hundred nanoseconds and the stencil hardly matters. From four dimensions it decides everything: the cost per evaluation follows the stencil's $w^N$, so the wide kernels fall two orders of magnitude behind the cubic B-spline in five dimensions, and `:a3`, which has the cubic's stencil, evaluates somewhat slower than it. The accuracy, by contrast, does not depend on the dimension at all: a tensor product keeps each axis's order, so at a fixed per-axis resolution each method's error is the same number from two dimensions to five, and the order shows as the ratio between the rows — `:b7` two orders of magnitude below the cubic, `:a4` one, `:a3` level with it. Which is the trade of the page: in many dimensions, order costs $w^N$ per point and buys the same accuracy it buys in one — which is why the default kernel narrows with the dimension, from `:b7` in one and two dimensions to `:b5` in three and `:a4` in four and five. ## Convergence and time to accuracy in three dimensions Three dimensions, from 11 to 81 knots per axis, each method evaluated at a hundred thousand random points. Left, the largest error as the grid is refined; right, the time to construct and to evaluate at the hundred thousand points against that error, which is the cost of a given accuracy when the interpolant is used in earnest. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The three-dimensional study"} ns3 = [11, 21, 41, 81] tp3 = testpoints(3, 100_000) res3 = Dict() # (name, n) => (time to construct and evaluate, error) for n in ns3 ax = axes_nd(3, n); v = values_nd(3, n) for (name, m) in methods_nd itp = m(ax, v) res3[(name, n)] = (time = (@b $m($ax, $v)).time + (@b evalpts($itp, $(tp3.P))).time, err = maximum(abs.(evalpts(itp, tp3.P) .- tp3.exact))) end end hs3 = 2 ./ (ns3 .- 1) fig = Figure(size = (800, 520)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate [s]") linkyaxes!(ax1, ax2) for (name, _) in methods_nd scatterlines!(ax1, hs3, [res3[(name, n)].err for n in ns3]; markersize = 8, label = name) scatterlines!(ax2, [res3[(name, n)].time for n in ns3], [res3[(name, n)].err for n in ns3]; markersize = 8) end Legend(fig[2, 1:2], ax1; orientation = :horizontal, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | largest error | 11³ | 21³ | 41³ | 81³ | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 2.6e-02 | 7.0e-03 | 1.8e-03 | 4.5e-04 | | Interpolations.jl cubic | 1.0e-03 | 2.5e-04 | 6.1e-05 | 5.8e-06 | | ConvInterp :a3 | 2.2e-03 | 1.9e-04 | 2.0e-05 | 2.4e-06 | | ConvInterp :a4 | 5.5e-04 | 2.4e-05 | 1.2e-06 | 6.8e-08 | | ConvInterp :b5 | 3.3e-04 | 9.8e-07 | 1.2e-08 | 8.0e-11 | | ConvInterp :b7 | 4.4e-04 | 7.2e-07 | 3.5e-09 | 2.0e-11 | | time to construct and evaluate | 11³ | 21³ | 41³ | 81³ | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 16.28 ms | 16.88 ms | 16.92 ms | 18.55 ms | | Interpolations.jl cubic | 18.08 ms | 21.90 ms | 20.61 ms | 187.47 ms | | ConvInterp :a3 | 19.57 ms | 21.12 ms | 32.43 ms | 34.43 ms | | ConvInterp :a4 | 32.76 ms | 25.54 ms | 24.67 ms | 47.79 ms | | ConvInterp :b5 | 50.91 ms | 40.05 ms | 40.79 ms | 67.78 ms | | ConvInterp :b7 | 66.96 ms | 63.40 ms | 53.01 ms | 83.04 ms | The time is dominated by the hundred thousand evaluations, so the right panel is the cost per point against the order. On the coarsest grid the cubic B-spline is the most accurate method per millisecond. From the next grid on, the picture inverts: `:a4`, `:b5` and `:b7` reach accuracies on 21³ and 41³ that the cubic does not reach on 81³, in a fraction of the time it takes there, because the cost per point grows with the stencil only once while the error falls with the order at every refinement. For an accuracy of one part in ten thousand or better in three dimensions, the kernels are the faster route; for a rough interpolant, the splines are. ## Lazy construction An eager interpolant copies the data into an array padded with ghost values along every axis, and the ghost values are the construction cost; a lazy one stores the data as they are and forms the ghost values it needs when a point near the boundary is evaluated. The same ghost values, so the two agree to rounding everywhere; the difference is where the work is done. Three grids with `:b7`, eager against lazy construction time, and which of the two the default chooses: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Eager against lazy construction"} cases = [(3, 100), (4, 30), (5, 12)] lz = map(cases) do (N, n) ax = axes_nd(N, n); v = values_nd(N, n) (N = N, n = n, eager = (@b convolution_interpolation($ax, $v; kernel = :b7, lazy = false)).time, lazy = (@b convolution_interpolation($ax, $v; kernel = :b7, lazy = true)).time, default = convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b7).itp.lazy isa Val{true} ? "lazy" : "eager") end; ``` ::: | grid | eager | lazy | speedup | default | |:--|--:|--:|--:|:--| | 3D 100³ | 9.84 ms | 2.4 μs | 4084× | eager | | 4D 30⁴ | 76.98 ms | 3.1 μs | 24831× | eager | | 5D 12⁵ | 352.81 ms | 3.7 μs | 94624× | eager | Lazy construction costs microseconds whatever the grid, since nothing is copied, while eager construction grows with the number of ghost values, which grows with the dimension and the kernel's width. The default, `lazy = nothing`, builds eagerly until eager construction would exceed either of two limits — $2^{27}$ values in the padded array, which is a gigabyte in `Float64`, or $2^{24}$ ghost values, which is about a second of construction — and lazily beyond them, so the three grids here are built eagerly by default, and a user who constructs many interpolants or evaluates few points sets `lazy = true` and pays nothing at construction. Evaluation in the interior is the same in both modes; near the boundary a lazy interpolant computes its ghost values on the fly, so eager is the faster choice when boundary cells are evaluated often. ## Choosing a kernel in many dimensions - The default kernel follows the dimension for this reason: `:b7` in one and two dimensions, `:b5` in three, `:a4` in four and five, `:a3` from six — the widest kernel whose stencil is still cheap at that dimension. - Where more accuracy is wanted than the default gives, a wider kernel buys it at the stencil's $w^N$ per evaluation, which the tables above put in numbers; where speed is wanted, `:a3` has the cubic B-spline's stencil and `:a1` the cheapest. - Build large grids lazily; the default does so beyond its limits, and `lazy = true` always works. - A grid uniform along some axes and nonuniform along others, or with different kernels per axis, costs each axis its own kernel's width and no more; the [concept page](../../concepts/interpolation.qmd) has the per-axis keywords. --- *Rendered with Julia 1.13.3 on a Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF machine (28 threads), with ConvolutionInterpolations.jl 1.0.2, Interpolations.jl 0.16.3, BSplineKit.jl 0.19.3, Dierckx.jl 0.5.4, FastChebInterp.jl 1.3.1, NumericalIntegration.jl 0.3.4, HCubature.jl 1.8.0, QuadGK.jl 2.11.3, ScatteredInterpolation.jl 0.3.6, NaturalNeighbours.jl 1.3.6, Chairmarks.jl 1.3.1.*
